reviewerDerivedProposition: A confirmed venous blood lead level of 18 mcg/dL is elevated but well below the chelation threshold. The correct response is environmental and nutritional education aimed at removing the exposure and reducing absorption, together with scheduled repeat venous testing. It is neither a normal result, nor an indication for inpatient chelation, nor a situation in which activated charcoal has any role.

clinicalVerdict: Correct and verified against the CDC clinical guidance for childhood lead exposure. For a confirmed venous level in the 10-19 mcg/dL band, CDC's follow-up table specifies early follow-up testing at 1-3 months and later follow-up at 3-6 months, with management including environmental investigation, iron-deficiency screening, nutritional counselling, developmental assessment and health-department reporting. Keyed option A states exactly the 1-to-3-month repeat venous test plus environmental education and is correct. Chelation is reserved for levels at or above 45 mcg/dL, so distractor B is correctly excluded and the rationale's threshold is right. The CDC blood lead reference value of 3.5 mcg/dL cited in the stage exhibit is current, so distractor C is correctly wrong. Activated charcoal does not bind lead, so distractor D is correctly wrong and is a genuine error rather than filler. The item's rationale also correctly frames education plus retesting as the standard for the 3.5 to 44 mcg/dL range. I found no clinical error, no invented fact and no unsupported premise.
